card.field: social sciences research on digital engagement and national identity (Palestinian context)

sections.text:
A. Published Materials
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(3) requires "[p]ublished material in professional or
major trade publications or major media about the alien, relating to the alien's work in the field for
which classification is sought, which shall include the title, date, and author ofsuch published material,
and any necessary translation." USCIS first determines whether the published material was related to
the person and the person's specific work in the field for which classification is sought. 3 USCIS then
determines whether the publication qualifies as a professional publication, major trade publication, or
major media publication. 4
The Petitioner argues the Beneficiary's eligibility for this criterion based on three articles posted on
gulfnews.com, zawya.com, and menafn.com. However, none ofthe articles reflect published material
about the Beneficiary relating to her work. For gulfnews.com, the article quotes the Beneficiary about

Moreover, the Petitioner did not establish that the articles appeared in professional or major trade
publications or major media. In evaluating whether a submitted publication is a professional
publication, major trade publication, or major media, relevant factors include the intended audience
(for professional and major trade publications) and the relative circulation, readership, or viewership
(for major trade publications and other major media). 5 Although the Petitioner argues that
gulfnews.com has "8.27 million monthly average page views," zawya.com's "official website boasts
over 573,000 monthly average page views," and menafn.com's "official website boasts over 225,000
monthly average page views," the Petitioner did not contextualize these figures. Similarly, the
Petitioner presented other evidence relating to rankings and statistics for the websites, such as
gulfnews.com and zawya.com receiving global rankings of 75,250 and 572,842, respectively. Again,
the Petitioner did not show the significance of these global rankings. The Petitioner did not establish
that these particular monthly average page views or global rankings place these websites at a level
consistent with "major" trade publications or media. 6 Cf, Branski v. Seng, No. 24-CV-360, 2024 WL
4678939, at *5 (E.D. Wis. Nov. 4, 2024) (indicating that the failure to provide context to circulation
figures makes it difficult to assess their significance).
For the reasons discussed above, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary fulfills this
criterion.

B. Contributions
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's original
scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major significance in the field." Analysis
under this criterion focuses on whether the beneficiary's original work constitutes major, significant
contributions in the field. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
5 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
6 The Petitioner does not claim that any of these websites qualify as professional publications, nor does the record support
it.
3
The Petitioner argues that the Beneficiary "was invited to present her original research at prestigious
international conferences." Evidence that the beneficiary's work was fonded, patented, or published,
while potentially demonstrating the work's originality, will not necessarily establish, on its own, that
the work is of major significance in the field. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at
M.4(C)(2). Although the Petitioner offered evidence of the Beneficiary's presentations at three
conferences, the Petitioner did not contextualize or show the impact of her presentations in the field.
The Petitioner did not demonstrate, for example, that any of her presentations resulted in majorly
significant contributions in the field. While the Petitioner contends that "[t]he fact that the Beneficiary
was invited to such prestigious conferences shows the originality of her work and major significance
to the industry," without supporting documentation showing the impact, influence, or effect in the
field in a majorly significant manner, the Petitioner did not establish that simply presenting original
work at conferences, even at prestigious ones, indicates original contributions ofmajor significance in
the field. Cf,Agrawal v. Miller, No. 4:24CV3143, 2025 WL 2879217, at *20 (D. Neb. Sept. 12, 2025)
(upholding that attendance and presentation of material at conferences is not uncommon in the
scientific fields, nor is the publication of research in the field).
Regarding the Beneficiary's overall citation record, the Petitioner initially provided her Google
Scholar profiles and, in response to SCOPS' RFE, from July 2025. Her most recent profile reflected
89 citations to her co-authored publications, with her three highest-cited articles receiving 46, 20, and
16 citations, respectively.7 The record, however, does not establish how many of these are self­
citations by her or her coauthors. Nonetheless, this criterion requires a petitioner to establish the
beneficiary's original contributions of major significance in the field. Thus, the burden is on the
petitioner to identify the original contributions and explain how or why they are considered to be of
major significance in the field. Here, the Petitioner did not show the significance of the Beneficiary's
citations to her individual papers or that her papers received citations compared to other articles the
field views as majorly significant. Documentation that published research has been highly cited
relative to other works in that field may be probative of the significance of the beneficiary's
contributions to the field of endeavor. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2);
cf, Gadhave, 2023 WL 6931334, at *5 (finding the record contained little evidence that contextualized
the number of citations the work had received).
Further, the Petitioner provided 2024 data from Clarivate Analytics (InCites Essential Science
Indicators) regarding baseline citation rates and percentiles by year of publication highlighting the
"Social Sciences, General." The Petitioner contends that "[ a ]ccording to a respectable research
analytics company, Clarivate Analytics, [the Beneficiary's] all-time citation count places her among
the top 10% of all cited researcher in the field of social sciences." However, the Petitioner again did
not indicate whether it factored in any self-citations in determining these percentile rankings.
Regardless, the Petitioner did not demonstrate how the Beneficiary's cumulative number of citations
represents contributions of major significance in the field. Moreover, aggregate citation figures tend
to reflect an individual's overall publication record rather than identifying which research or findings,
if any, the field considers to be majorly significant. In addition, the documentation from Clarivate
Analytics states that "[c ]itation frequency is highly skewed, with many infrequently cited papers and
relatively few highly cited papers. Consequently, citation rates should not be interpreted as
representing the central tendency of the distribution." Therefore, considering Clarivate Analytics'
7 Three of the Beneficiary's other articles received three or less citations, and her other eight articles received no citations.
4
admission of highly skewed data, the Petitioner did not show the reliability of the figures, and
therefore, reflects very little, if any, probative value.
Moreover, citation frequency, which is quantitative in nature, does not reveal the reasons for the
citations, which involve a qualitative analysis. In other words, a high citation number might show that
others in the field have noticed the Beneficiary's work, but it does not confirm that such work or
research has risen to the level of major significance. Regarding a qualitative analysis of the citations,
while they may indicate some degree of interest in her research from her colleagues and peers in the
field, this evidence is not sufficient without supporting material to demonstrate a degree considered to
be majorly significant. Cf, Agrawal, 2025 WL 2879217, at *20 (upholding that plaintiff did not
provide evidence demonstrating that work has been widely cited); Bhanu v. Garland, No. CV 22-103,
2023 WL 6119357, at *7-8 (E.D. Pa. Sept. 18, 2023) (upholding plaintiff did not demonstrate the
number of citations received by his published articles reflect a level of interest in his work from
relevant parties to meet this criterion); Gadhave, 2023 WL 6931334, at *5 (finding the record
contained little evidence that contextualized the number of citations the work had received); Jafarov
v. United States Citizenship & Immigr. Servs., No. 23 CIV. 3372 (PAE), 2024 WL 69056, *7 (S.D.N.Y.
Jan. 5, 2024) ( finding the absence ofdetail about the actual impact ofthe work and the limited citations
the work had thus far received meant that he did not satisfy this criterion).
Finally, the Petitioner references a few recommendation letters. However, the letters are not
sufficiently persuasive. The letters generally highlight the Beneficiary's work and opine on its
importance but not elaborate and demonstrate how her work is considered to be majorly significant.
For example, J-V-P- indicated that "[p]olicymakers and cultural institutions rely on these findings to
develop more nuanced strategies for digital engagement."8 J-V-P- did not, for instance, identify any
strategies that were developed, if any, based on the Beneficiary's findings or how the overall field has
been significantly impacted or influenced in a major way. Cf, Visinscaia, 4 F. Supp. 3d at 134 (finding
the term "major significance in the field" can be reasonably interpreted to mean that there must be
some impact "in the field as a whole"); see also Hristov v. Roark, No. 09-CV-2731, 2011 WL4711885,
at *11 (E.D.N.Y. Sep. 30, 2011); Skokos v. United States Dep't of Homeland Sec., No.
209CV00193RLHPAL, 2010 WL 11538054, at *4 (D. Nev. Jan. 13, 2010), ajf'd sub nom. Skokos v.
US. Dep't ofHomeland Sec., 420 F. App'x 712 (9th Cir. 2011).
Similarly, R-F- claimed that the Beneficiary's "work has led to a reconceptualization of national
identity and self-representation in the Palestinian context." In discussing the effect in the field, R-F­
referenced her presentations and panel discussions. However, R-F- did not elaborate and detail how
the presentations or panel discussions resulted in any measurable impact of the Beneficiary's work in
the field. As indicated above, simply authoring material or making conference presentations is
insufficient to meet this criterion without evidence that the findings or research from publications or
conferences caused majorly significant contributions. Cf, Agrawal, 2025 WL 2879217, at *20
(upholding that attendance and presentation of material at conferences is not uncommon in the
scientific fields, nor is the publication of research in the field).
Detailed letters from experts in the field explaining the nature and significance of the beneficiary's
contribution may also provide valuable context for evaluating the claimed original contributions of
8 Although we discuss a sample of letters, we have reviewed and considered each in the record.
5
major significance, particularly when the record includes documentation corroborating the claimed
significance. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2). Submitted letters should
specifically describe the beneficiary's contribution and its significance in the field and should set forth
the basis of the writer's knowledge and expertise. Id. Here, the letters point to the Beneficiary's work
but do not demonstrate how the field views it as original contributions of major significance in the
field, such as widespread impact or influence. Cf, Gadhave, 2023 WL 6931334, at *5 (finding
testimonial letters contained mostly general, conclusory statements about the value of the person's
research without explaining in detail specific ways in which his contributions have already been
widely applied or replicated to serve the industry); Jafarov, 2024 WL 69056, at *8 (finding testimonial
evidence spoke largely in generalities and did not evidence the tangible impact of his work in the
field); Noroozi v. Napolitano, 905 F. Supp. 2d 535, 544 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) (upholding reference letters
with limited detail on satisfaction of regulatory criterion insufficient to form the basis for required
evidence).
For the reasons discussed above, considered both individually and collectively, the Petitioner did not
demonstrate the Beneficiary meets this criterion.
